info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 6.1: Manual Normalization, Abbreviations, and Editorial Policy.

name.text: 01 Question: The Problem Normalization Solves and Creates

questiontext.text: Why does standardizing the spelling of a historical manuscript create a scholarly dilemma?

generalfeedback.text: Standardizing spelling makes historical documents digitally searchable, but silent modernization destroys crucial linguistic, dialectal, and scribal evidence.

answer.text: Standardization makes text searchable and computationally parsable, but silent modernization destroys crucial linguistic, dialectal, and scribal evidence.

feedback.text: Correct. Variant spellings are vital historical evidence; TEI resolves this dilemma by keeping diplomatic and regularized forms in parallel.

answer.text: Standardization increases the byte size of digital files beyond what modern web servers can deliver.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File size is not the issue; the concern is the permanent loss of historical and linguistic evidence.

answer.text: Standardization causes optical character recognition tools to misidentify subsequent document pages.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization is an editorial markup process, not an image recognition task.

answer.text: Standardization forces the editor to eliminate all XML attributes from the TEI header.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization concerns the transcription text within , not the header metadata.

name.text: 02 Question: The Scholarly Dilemma: Preservation vs. Accessibility

questiontext.text: How does digital text encoding resolve the conflict between physical documentary fidelity and modern reader accessibility?

generalfeedback.text: Digital text encoding resolves the conflict between preservation and accessibility by maintaining diplomatic and normalized layers in parallel within a single document.

answer.text: It allows diplomatic and normalized layers to coexist simultaneously within a single data structure, letting readers or software select the desired view.

feedback.text: Correct. Digital encoding eliminates the need to choose between a pure diplomatic facsimile and a modernized reading text by storing both in parallel.

answer.text: It forces editors to publish two completely separate physical books with different ISBNs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital editions encode both layers within the same digital file rather than splitting them into separate physical editions.

answer.text: It automatically translates all historical languages into modern English using machine learning.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization standardizes historical orthography within the same language; it is not automatic language translation.

answer.text: It requires readers to install specialized database servers before opening a text file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Parallel TEI markup is rendered seamlessly in standard web browsers and XML players.

name.text: 03 Question: The TEI Resolution: Parallel Layers with <choice>

questiontext.text: What is the primary function of the TEI element in digital textual editing?

generalfeedback.text: The TEI element acts as a transparent container that holds original witness readings and modern editorial regularizations side by side.

answer.text: It acts as a container grouping alternative encodings of the same textual unit, such as an original spelling alongside a regularized modern form.

feedback.text: Correct. transparently wraps multiple representations of the same word or phrase without subordinating or destroying the original reading.

answer.text: It forces the student to answer a multiple-choice quiz question before proceeding to the next page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Despite its name, TEI is an editorial markup container, not an interactive quiz element.

answer.text: It randomly selects one of several spellings each time the digital webpage is refreshed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. provides structured, permanent alternatives for user toggling or targeted indexing, not random display.

answer.text: It validates whether the XML document conforms strictly to the TEI All schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validation is handled by tools like Jing or Scholarly XML, not by the element itself.

name.text: 04 Question: Orthographic Regularization: <orig> and <reg>

questiontext.text: When regularizing historical spelling in TEI, which child elements must be paired inside ?

generalfeedback.text: Pair and within a element to record historical orthography alongside modern standard spelling at word-level granularity.

answer.text: <orig> for the original witness spelling, and <reg> for the modern regularized spelling.

feedback.text: Correct. holds the diplomatic reading from the manuscript, and holds the modern editorial regularization.

answer.text: <abbr> for the original spelling, and <expan> for the regularized spelling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. and are reserved for abbreviations and expansions, not general spelling variation.

answer.text: <sic> for the historical spelling, and <corr> for the regularized spelling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. and are used exclusively for genuine scribal blunders, not acceptable historical spelling variants.

answer.text: <old> for the manuscript reading, and <new> for the modern headword.

feedback.text: Incorrect. and are not valid TEI elements; the standard elements are and .

name.text: 05 Question: Editorial Responsibility and the @resp Attribute

questiontext.text: Why is the @resp attribute attached to the element rather than the element?

generalfeedback.text: Always attach the @resp attribute to your regularized element to document who made the editorial intervention.

answer.text: The regularized form is an interpretive scholarly intervention supplied by the modern editor, whereas the original text belongs to the historical witness.

feedback.text: Correct. The editor did not create the historical spelling in ; they created the modernized interpretation in , so responsibility is attributed to .

answer.text: The XML specification forbids attaching attributes of any kind to tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. can carry attributes; @resp is placed on because regularization is an editorial act.

answer.text: Attaching @resp to would automatically trigger a schema validation error in VS Code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema allows @resp on both elements, but scholarly methodology requires attributing editorial interventions.

answer.text: The historical scribe's signature must always be placed inside the @resp attribute of .

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical scribes are identified in or , while @resp indicates the editor who normalized the form.

name.text: 06 Question: Abbreviations in Historical Documents

questiontext.text: What was the primary historical reason for the extensive use of abbreviations in medieval and early modern manuscripts?

generalfeedback.text: Historical abbreviations were practical tools for conserving expensive writing surfaces and speeding manual transcription, but they require digital expansion for modern accessibility.

answer.text: Writing surfaces like parchment were expensive, and clerks needed to maximize words per page and speed manual copying.

feedback.text: Correct. Parchment and paper were costly commodities, making graphic compression essential for conserving space and labor.

answer.text: Clerks abbreviated words to prevent ordinary people from reading official legal documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scribal abbreviations were standardized systems for efficiency and cost reduction, not secret ciphers.

answer.text: Guild regulations mandated that no document could contain words longer than seven characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No such guild regulations existed; abbreviations developed pragmatically across bureaucratic traditions.

answer.text: Early printing presses lacked the mechanical ability to cast full English words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Movable type could print full words; abbreviations were inherited directly from manual scribal culture.

name.text: 07 Question: Encoding Abbreviations: <abbr> and <expan>

questiontext.text: Which TEI markup correctly encodes a historical abbreviation and its editorial expansion?

generalfeedback.text: Use ...... to encode historical abbreviations and their full editorial expansions in parallel.

answer.text: <choice><abbr>Gov<hi rend='superscript'>r</hi></abbr><expan resp='#editor'>Governor</expan></choice>

feedback.text: Correct. The raw abbreviation is enclosed in and the full editorial expansion is enclosed in with @resp.

answer.text: <choice><orig>Govr</orig><reg resp='#editor'>Governor</reg></choice>

feedback.text: Incorrect. While syntactically valid XML, / is used for spelling variation; abbreviations must be tagged with /.

answer.text: <abbr expan='Governor'>Govr</abbr>

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI P5 uses parallel child elements within , rather than storing expansions in an @expan attribute.

answer.text: <choice><sic>Govr</sic><corr resp='#editor'>Governor</corr></choice>

feedback.text: Incorrect. An abbreviation is a conventional writing practice, not an error ().

name.text: 08 Question: Suspensions, Contractions, and Brevigraphs

questiontext.text: How does a scribal contraction differ from a scribal suspension?

generalfeedback.text: Historical abbreviations fall into three main types—suspensions, contractions, and brevigraphs—all of which are encoded using TEI and .

answer.text: A contraction retains the first and last letters while dropping internal letters; a suspension writes the start of the word and drops the end.

feedback.text: Correct. Contractions drop internal letters (often using superscripts), whereas suspensions truncate the ending.

answer.text: A contraction applies only to nouns, while a suspension applies exclusively to verbs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both abbreviation types apply across all grammatical parts of speech.

answer.text: A contraction is an accidental ink smudge, while a suspension is a deliberate editorial punctuation mark.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are deliberate, systematic historical abbreviation practices.

answer.text: A contraction was used only in printed books, while a suspension was used only in private handwriting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both conventions were used widely in manuscripts and early printed books alike.

name.text: 09 Question: Regularization vs. Correction: <reg> vs. <corr>

questiontext.text: Why must an editor avoid tagging historical spelling variants like 'publick' or 'étoit' with and ?

generalfeedback.text: Use / for acceptable historical and dialectal spelling variants, and reserve / strictly for genuine scribal blunders.

answer.text: Those spellings were acceptable, standard orthography in their historical periods; / is reserved strictly for genuine errors and blunders.

feedback.text: Correct. Using for valid historical variation is anachronistic and inaccurate; valid variation belongs in /.

answer.text: The TEI schema automatically deletes any tag found inside an English or French document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas validate grammar and syntax, not historical semantics.

answer.text: <sic> and <corr> can only be used when editing texts written before the invention of the printing press.

feedback.text: Incorrect. and are used across all periods for genuine blunders or misprints.

answer.text: Tagging a word with prevents web browsers from rendering any text on the screen.

feedback.text: Incorrect. renders normally in all standard stylesheets and digital edition viewers.

name.text: 10 Question: Case Study 1: 18th-Century Legal English (1752 Treaty)

questiontext.text: What typographic and orthographic feature is widely characteristic of 18th-century official legal broadsides like the 1752 Treaty?

generalfeedback.text: Eighteenth-century legal documents feature substantive noun capitalization, archaic terminal suffixes, and the long s, requiring clear editorial decisions about what to regularize.

answer.text: Capitalization of substantive common nouns, terminal archaic suffixes like -ck, and the use of the long s (ſ).

feedback.text: Correct. Eighteenth-century printed legal texts systematically capitalized common nouns and used archaic terminal spellings alongside the long s.

answer.text: Strict lowercase lettering throughout all paragraphs with zero capital letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Eighteenth-century printing favored heavy, substantive noun capitalization.

answer.text: The complete absence of punctuation marks, spaces, or paragraph breaks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Legal treaties were highly structured with formal articles, margins, and punctuation.

answer.text: Writing all legal terminology in ancient Coptic script rather than English roman type.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Colonial British treaties were printed in English roman type with occasional Latin phrases.

name.text: 11 Question: Archaic Contractions and Superscripts in Colonial Documents

questiontext.text: In colonial documents, why did clerks write 'ye' for the word 'the'?

generalfeedback.text: Early modern ye is a typographical substitution for the letter thorn, representing the word the, and should be encoded as an abbreviation with and .

answer.text: Early English printers lacked a type sort for the Old English letter thorn (þ) and substituted the visually similar letter y.

feedback.text: Correct. The y in 'ye' is a typographical surrogate for the thorn rune representing the 'th' sound; it was never pronounced with a y sound.

answer.text: Eighteenth-century English speakers pronounced the word 'the' with a hard 'y' consonant sound.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The pronunciation was always /ðə/ ('the'); the spelling reflects a font substitution.

answer.text: The King of England mandated that the word 'the' be spelled with a y in all North American colonies.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It was a centuries-old typographical convention, not a royal decree.

answer.text: Clerks wrote 'ye' because the letter 't' had been officially eliminated from legal alphabets.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The letter 't' was in continuous use across all colonial documents.

name.text: 12 Question: Case Study 2: 19th-Century Poetic Idiosyncrasy (Emily Dickinson)

questiontext.text: Why does normalizing capitalization in an autograph poem by Emily Dickinson require extreme editorial caution?

generalfeedback.text: Emily Dickinson's autograph poetry uses capitalization, dashes, and variant spellings as expressive artistic devices, requiring extreme caution during normalization.

answer.text: Her capitalized common nouns often represent deliberate personifications and rhythmic accents integral to her poetic meaning.

feedback.text: Correct. Dickinson's capitals convey intentional poetic emphasis; standardizing them to lowercase flattens her literary expression.

answer.text: Her manuscripts were printed on machine-punched cards that cannot be edited in XML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dickinson wrote by hand on manuscript paper, which is encoded in standard TEI XML.

answer.text: Dickinson specifically stated in her will that anyone who changed a letter would face legal prosecution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The caution stems from scholarly respect for poetic voice, not legal threats.

answer.text: The TEI Guidelines strictly ban the use of tags inside any text labeled as poetry.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The TEI provides elements for poetry, but literary editors exercise restraint to protect authorial intent.

name.text: 13 Question: When NOT to Normalize: The Poetic Boundary

questiontext.text: What major damage was inflicted on Emily Dickinson's poetry by 19th-century post-mortem print editors?

generalfeedback.text: Editorial restraint is essential: never normalize capitalization, punctuation, or spelling that carries intentional poetic or stylistic meaning.

answer.text: They replaced her characteristic dashes with conventional commas and smoothed her irregular capitalization to conform to standard Victorian hymnal meter.

feedback.text: Correct. Early editors regularized her unique punctuation and capitalization, altering the rhythm and psychological tension of her poems.

answer.text: They burned all original manuscript copies to prevent scholars from seeing her handwriting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The manuscripts survived at Amherst and Harvard, allowing modern scholars to restore her original readings.

answer.text: They translated all of her poems into Latin without publishing the English text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They published English editions, but heavily modernized her orthography and punctuation.

answer.text: They forced her poems into strict 30-section TEI XML files that failed validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML was invented a century after the first print editions of Dickinson.

name.text: 14 Question: Case Study 3: 20th-Century Vernacular Writing (Maud Lewis)

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents a typical orthographic feature found in Maud Lewis's personal correspondence?

generalfeedback.text: Personal letters by vernacular writers like Maud Lewis feature phonetic spellings and omitted apostrophes that can be regularized for readability while preserving their authenticity.

answer.text: Phonetic spelling variants like 'allways' or 'untill', and unpunctuated contractions like 'dont' or 'cant'.

feedback.text: Correct. Lewis's letters reflect informal vernacular English with phonetic consonant doubling and omitted apostrophes.

answer.text: Extensive Greek marginalia written in polytonic Hellenistic script.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lewis wrote personal English correspondence in rural Nova Scotia.

answer.text: Strict adherence to 18th-century French court abbreviation protocols.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Her correspondence is vernacular Canadian folk writing, unrelated to 18th-century French courts.

answer.text: Machine-encoded cryptographic ciphers used to communicate with art galleries.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Her handwriting is informal and personal, containing ordinary spoken phonetic spellings.

name.text: 15 Question: Respecting the Vernacular Voice

questiontext.text: Why should an editor use / rather than / when encoding vernacular spellings in working-class correspondence?

generalfeedback.text: Treat vernacular writing with scholarly respect: use / to aid digital search, but never use or alter an author's authentic regional grammar.

answer.text: Vernacular spellings reflect authentic dialectal phonology and literacy practices; treating them as 'errors' reflects linguistic bias.

feedback.text: Correct. Dialectal and vernacular spellings are legitimate sociolinguistic data, not broken blunders requiring patronizing correction.

answer.text: <sic> is only allowed when transcribing texts written by government officials or monarchs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. is used for errors regardless of the author's social status, but vernacular variation is not an error.

answer.text: Using automatically instructs modern speech synthesizers to speak with a Nova Scotian accent.

feedback.text: Incorrect. provides standard lexical spellings for search and indexing, not regional audio synthesis.

answer.text: The TEI schema completely disallows the use of inside personal letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The schema allows , but editorial methodology advises against mischaracterizing dialect as blunder.

name.text: 16 Question: Case Study 4: 18th-Century Revolutionary French (1791 Decree)

questiontext.text: What major historical orthographic shift is commonly found in 18th-century French documents like the 1791 Decree?

generalfeedback.text: Eighteenth-century French documents systematically write oi where modern French writes ai, an orthographic shift that is cleanly normalized using and .

answer.text: Imperfect verb endings and adjectives written with 'oi' (e.g., 'étoit', 'françois') where modern French writes 'ai' ('était', 'français').

feedback.text: Correct. The Voltairean spelling reform replacing historical 'oi' with phonetic 'ai' was codified by the Académie in 1835.

answer.text: The complete elimination of all vowels in favor of consonant-only abbreviations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. French legal decrees used standard Romance vowel systems with conventional legal shorthand.

answer.text: The substitution of English legal phrases for all French royal statutes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The National Assembly promulgated decrees in French, retaining legal Latin terms like L.S.

answer.text: Writing every sentence backwards to prevent counter-revolutionary sabotage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Revolutionary decrees were official public laws intended for widespread civic proclamation.

name.text: 17 Question: Historical Precedents: Phonological Drift and Sound Mergers

questiontext.text: What universal linguistic phenomenon explains why historical texts across languages exhibit systematic spelling variations?

generalfeedback.text: Orthographic variation is the natural historical result of spoken pronunciation changing faster than conservative written spelling.

answer.text: Spoken pronunciation evolves continuously over time, while written orthography tends to remain conservative and frozen.

feedback.text: Correct. Sound shifts (such as Greek iotacism or the English Great Vowel Shift) create mismatches between spoken sounds and traditional spellings.

answer.text: Ancient governments intentionally scrambled alphabets every century to confuse rival nations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Spelling variation arises naturally through phonetic sound changes and scribal practice, not political conspiracies.

answer.text: Writers across history had identical pronunciations and simply made random typographical mistakes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Spelling variations often reflect highly systematic phonological shifts, not random blunders.

answer.text: Parchment deterioration causes letters to transform physically into different alphabetical characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ink and parchment fade, but sound shifts are human linguistic processes.

name.text: 18 Question: Punctuation and Spacing Variations

questiontext.text: How should a digital editor handle historical compound word divisions, such as 'to morrow' written as two words?

generalfeedback.text: Spacing variations and compound word divisions can be regularized within , but historical punctuation should be modified with great restraint.

answer.text: Wrap the multi-word unit in , placing 'to morrow' in and 'tomorrow' in .

feedback.text: Correct. TEI can wrap multi-token groups to bridge historical spacing differences with modern compound words.

answer.text: Delete the space directly in the manuscript using an image-editing eraser tool.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors never alter archival images; TEI captures spacing non-destructively through markup.

answer.text: Insert a page break tag between the two words to force a line reset.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A marks a physical page boundary, not a word division.

answer.text: Refuse to encode the line because the TEI schema forbids spaces inside tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Spaces are completely valid inside tags.

name.text: 19 Question: Nesting and Combining TEI Elements

questiontext.text: What is the recommended practical approach when an abbreviated word also features an archaic historical spelling?

generalfeedback.text: While TEI permits nesting inside , practical editing favors the simplest clean markup that captures the necessary scholarly distinction.

answer.text: Supply the modern standardized form directly inside , avoiding overly verbose nested tags.

feedback.text: Correct. While nesting inside is valid XML, expanding directly to the modern form provides cleaner, more readable markup.

answer.text: Delete both the abbreviation and the word, replacing them with a element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A represents missing or illegible text, not a word requiring normalization.

answer.text: Invent an unauthorized XML tag like that merges all three functions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inventing non-standard elements breaks TEI schema validation.

answer.text: Refuse to expand any abbreviation that contains more than two letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Abbreviations of any length can be expanded systematically in TEI.

name.text: 20 Question: Milestones Inside Normalization Blocks

questiontext.text: When a historical word divided across a line break is regularized, where does the milestone tag belong?

generalfeedback.text: Physical milestone tags like belong inside the element because line breaks exist in the physical witness, not in the abstract regularized lemma.

answer.text: Inside the element, because the physical line break occurred on the manuscript witness, not in the abstract modern lemma.

feedback.text: Correct. Physical milestones belong to the physical document layer (), leaving as an uninterrupted lexical string.

answer.text: Outside the element, dividing the entire tag into two broken halves.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Splitting creates malformed XML and disconnects the regularized word.

answer.text: Inside the element, forcing the modern reading to display a hyphen.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The modern lemma is an abstract word that does not have a physical line break.

answer.text: Line break tags must be permanently deleted whenever a word is regularized.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical line breaks are essential codicological data and must never be deleted.

name.text: 21 Question: Formulating an Editorial Policy

questiontext.text: Why must an editor formulate an explicit written Editorial Policy before regularizing a document?

generalfeedback.text: An explicit, written editorial policy is mandatory to ensure that all normalizations are consistent, defensible, and reproducible.

answer.text: An explicit policy establishes clear boundaries and target authorities, preventing arbitrary, inconsistent personal whims from corrupting the dataset.

feedback.text: Correct. Without a stated policy, editorial choices fluctuate with human fatigue, creating unreliable and inconsistent data.

answer.text: An editorial policy is legally required by international copyright law before opening XML files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a scholarly methodological necessity for data integrity, not a copyright statute.

answer.text: A written policy is needed only if the editor plans to sell the digital edition for commercial profit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. All academic digital scholarly editions require transparent editorial declarations.

answer.text: Writing a policy automatically inserts all tags into the XML document without typing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The policy guides human and automated choices; it does not replace the encoding process.

name.text: 22 Question: The Principle of Consistency

questiontext.text: What is the primary risk of inconsistent normalization across a digital text corpus?

generalfeedback.text: Consistency is the cardinal rule of digital editing: an editor must apply their stated regularization policy systematically to every occurrence in the text.

answer.text: It skews quantitative lexical and concordance searches, producing inaccurate statistical frequencies for downstream researchers.

feedback.text: Correct. If half the instances of an archaic word are normalized and half are missed, quantitative corpus research becomes unreliable.

answer.text: It causes the computer operating system to corrupt the hard drive sectors storing the XML file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inconsistent editorial markup affects textual scholarship, not computer hardware.

answer.text: It permanently prevents the TEI Header from recording the author's name.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The TEI header records metadata independently of body text consistency.

answer.text: It forces the validator to reject all subsequent image files uploaded to the repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Image files and XML text validation are separate pipeline stages.

name.text: 23 Question: Building the Editorial Rule Ledger

questiontext.text: What is an Editorial Rule Ledger in digital textual scholarship?

generalfeedback.text: Maintain an explicit Editorial Rule Ledger with unique rule IDs and clear rationales to track every transformation applied to your text.

answer.text: A structured table cataloguing every active regularization rule, its input pattern, regularized replacement, and scholarly rationale.

feedback.text: Correct. The Rule Ledger acts as the master blueprint for manual encoding, regular expressions, and AI auditing.

answer.text: A financial accounting spreadsheet used to track the cost of server hosting.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An Editorial Rule Ledger tracks textual transformations, not financial accounts.

answer.text: A private cryptographic key used to encrypt student grades in Moodle.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is an open, auditable record of editorial standardization rules.

answer.text: A legal contract signed between the archival library and the software developer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The ledger documents scholarly regularization decisions within the project repository.

name.text: 24 Question: Categorizing Regularization Rules

questiontext.text: Why is it beneficial to categorize rules into orthographic, abbreviation, typographical, and casing groups?

generalfeedback.text: Categorize your rules into orthographic, abbreviation, typographical, and casing groups to ensure appropriate TEI tagging.

answer.text: It prevents category confusion and ensures that replacement patterns generate the correct TEI elements ( vs. ).

feedback.text: Correct. Categorization maps each linguistic phenomenon to its proper TEI tag pair (/ versus /).

answer.text: The TEI schema requires all XML files to contain exactly four separate elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A TEI document typically contains one ; categorization organizes editorial rules.

answer.text: Uncategorized rules cause VS Code to crash whenever a search is conducted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code searches uncategorized text normally, but structured rules prevent human error.

answer.text: Categorizing rules allows editors to skip validation checks during Moodle export.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validation is always required regardless of rule categorization.

name.text: 25 Question: Documenting the Policy in the TEI Header

questiontext.text: Where in the TEI Header should an editor formally declare their normalization policy?

generalfeedback.text: Record your editorial policy inside the and elements of your TEI Header, declaring method='markup' for non-destructive transparency.

answer.text: Inside within the and elements, declaring method='markup'.

feedback.text: Correct. The element formally records editorial practices, and method='markup' declares non-destructive tagging.

answer.text: Inside within the element, declaring status='secret'.

feedback.text: Incorrect. records publisher and licensing information, not editorial normalization methods.

answer.text: Inside within the element, declaring language='python'.

feedback.text: Incorrect. documents the historical date and place of original composition.

answer.text: At the very end of inside a hidden HTML comment block.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Formal TEI metadata belongs in dedicated header elements, not trailing comments.

name.text: 26 Question: Manual Normalization in VS Code

questiontext.text: Why does Step 1 of the normalization module require hand-encoding in VS Code before using automated tools?

generalfeedback.text: Manual normalization in VS Code builds editorial discipline by requiring you to evaluate every word against your explicit policy ledger.

answer.text: Hand-encoding builds editorial discipline, forcing the editor to closely evaluate every word against the policy and discover unstated edge cases.

feedback.text: Correct. Manual work establishes the essential human baseline and reveals ambiguities that automated scripts overlook.

answer.text: Modern computers lack the processing power to run automated regular expressions without human pre-typing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Computers execute regex in milliseconds; manual encoding is a deliberate pedagogical and methodological step.

answer.text: The TEI Consortium fines academic institutions that use automated tools without manual pre-approval.

feedback.text: Incorrect. There are no fines or bureaucratic bans; manual ground truth is a scientific best practice.

answer.text: Hand-encoding is required because VS Code does not support regular expression search.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code has a powerful built-in regex engine, which will be introduced on Wednesday.

name.text: 27 Question: Keyboard Shortcuts and Snippets for <choice>

questiontext.text: How can an editor streamline manual XML encoding in VS Code without sacrificing human judgment?

generalfeedback.text: Configure custom VS Code XML snippets to automate the repetitive typing of structures while keeping every editorial decision under manual human control.

answer.text: By creating custom user snippets in VS Code that expand short prefixes into pre-formatted templates around selected text.

feedback.text: Correct. Custom snippets eliminate repetitive tag typing while keeping every editorial decision under manual human control.

answer.text: By permanently turning off XML schema validation in the VS Code settings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Disabling validation hides syntax errors and produces broken XML files.

answer.text: By writing the entire transcription in Microsoft Word and pasting it into VS Code.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Microsoft Word introduces smart quotes and non-standard formatting that corrupt XML.

answer.text: By delegating the transcription to an unmonitored background bot without reviewing the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unmonitored automation defeats the purpose of human baseline creation.

name.text: 28 Question: Validating Normalized TEI against the Schema

questiontext.text: What should an editor do if a newly inserted block displays a red squiggly underline in VS Code?

generalfeedback.text: Constantly monitor the VS Code Problems panel to ensure that every newly inserted block validates with zero schema errors.

answer.text: Hover over the tag to read the schema validation error, check for unclosed tags or invalid child elements, and consult the Problems panel.

feedback.text: Correct. The Problems panel and hover tooltips identify the exact syntax or structural violation according to the active RELAX NG schema.

answer.text: Immediately delete the entire paragraph to make the red underline disappear.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The error should be diagnosed and corrected, not solved by destroying text.

answer.text: Ignore the underline because TEI schemas do not recognize the element.

feedback.text: Incorrect. is a core TEI element; an error indicates invalid children, attributes, or unclosed tags.

answer.text: Restart the computer operating system to clear the editor's visual cache.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validation errors reflect real syntax problems in the document markup.

name.text: 29 Question: Preparing Your Manual Ground Truth for Wednesday

questiontext.text: Why is today's hand-encoded 20-line passage described as a 'Ground Truth' baseline?

generalfeedback.text: Your hand-encoded manual passage serves as the indispensable ground truth baseline against which Wednesday's regular expressions and Friday's AI outputs will be rigorously evaluated.

answer.text: It represents the verified gold standard of scholarly judgment against which Wednesday's regular expressions and Friday's AI passes will be measured.

feedback.text: Correct. Without an independently verified manual baseline, an editor cannot calculate true positives, false positives, or hypercorrections.

answer.text: It is called ground truth because it must be carved into a physical stone tablet before submission.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ground truth is a scientific term for an independently verified reference dataset.

answer.text: It is a legal term indicating that the document has been approved by the Supreme Court.

feedback.text: Incorrect. In data science and digital humanities, ground truth denotes the benchmark reference data.

answer.text: It means that no other person is ever allowed to read or criticize the transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ground truth datasets are shared and audited openly in peer review.

name.text: 30 Question: Review and Workshop 6 Step 1 Checklist

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a mandatory deliverable for Step 1 of Workshop 6?

generalfeedback.text: Completing Step 1 establishes a validated manual ground truth and an explicit rule ledger, preparing you to automate and audit normalization throughout the rest of the week.

answer.text: A 20-line excerpt encoded with validated TEI markup, accompanied by a documented Editorial Rule Ledger in NORMALIZATION.md.

feedback.text: Correct. Step 1 requires the hand-encoded TEI excerpt and the explicit policy rule ledger establishing the ground truth baseline.

answer.text: A 5,000-line Python script that automatically deletes all historical abbreviations from the repository.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Step 1 is manual; automated rules are explored on Wednesday.

answer.text: A signed legal waiver transferring ownership of the manuscript to the university library.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Student workshops involve open pedagogical exercises on public historical documents.

answer.text: A 30-slide PowerPoint presentation with custom voiceover recordings for each section.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The deliverables are the validated TEI XML file and the markdown rule ledger.
